newsitem.title: UK: British cabinet embroiled in row, slumps in polls.
newsitem.headline: British cabinet embroiled in row, slumps in polls.

text.p: Britain's Conservative government slumped in opinion polls on Friday and was hit by a bitter cabinet row that dealt another blow to its re-election chances.
With a general election less than two months away, the latest Gallup opinion poll showed the Conservatives were trailing 26 percentage points behind the opposition Labour Party.
It was the worst rating recorded by a ruling party in the last weeks of a parliament. One in three people polled by Gallup for the Daily Telegraph felt the government was "on its last legs".
The Conservatives, in power since 1979, are bidding for their fifth election win in a row.
But a Harris poll in the Independent newspaper underlined what a mountain they have to climb -- it said they were 21 points behind Labour.

Prime Minister John Major, his party riven by divisions over Britain's role in the European Union, has been battling to present a united front in the run-up to the general election he must call by May.
But cabinet squabbling erupted between Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg and Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth in yet another damaging row over food safety.

Hogg, already under fire over his handling of the mad cow crisis, denied in parliament he had suppressed a damaging report on unhealthy conditions in abattoirs that could have spread disease to meat supplies.

Professor Hugh Pennington, the scientist appointed by the government to look into an E.coli food poisoning outbreak that has killed 20 people in Scotland, said he had not been told about the report and that it could have helped him in his investigation.

Forsyth's office underlined a sense of cabinet disarray. It took the highly unusual step of putting out a curt statement on Thursday night which said: "Scottish office ministers were not aware of the report and have still not seen a copy."

The Labour Party said it believed the government may have held the report back because it would have come on top of a ministerial admission of a possible link between mad cow disease, or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), and its human equivalent Creutzfeld-Jakob Disease (CJD).

The crisis over mad cow disease resulted in a European Union worldwide ban on British beef exports. The ban has crippled the country's beef industry and led to two widespread culling operations which have cost the government 3.5 billion pounds ($5.7 billion).
